292## Improving the skill
294This is the heart of the loop. You've run the test cases, the user has reviewed the results, and now you need to make the skill better based on their feedback.
296### How to think about improvements
2981. **Generalize from the feedback.** The big picture thing that's happening here is that we're trying to create skills that can be used a million times (maybe literally, maybe even more who knows) across many different prompts. Here you and the user are iterating on only a few examples over and over again because it helps move faster. The user knows these examples in and out and it's quick for them to assess new outputs. But if the skill you and the user are codeveloping works only for those examples, it's useless. Rather than put in fiddly overfitty changes, or oppressively constrictive MUSTs, if there's some stubborn issue, you might try branching out and using different metaphors, or recommending different patterns of working. It's relatively cheap to try and maybe you'll land on something great.
3002. **Keep the prompt lean.** Remove things that aren't pulling their weight. Make sure to read the transcripts, not just the final outputs — if it looks like the skill is making the model waste a bunch of time doing things that are unproductive, you can try getting rid of the parts of the skill that are making it do that and seeing what happens.
3023. **Explain the why.** Try hard to explain the **why** behind everything you're asking the model to do. Today's LLMs are *smart*. They have good theory of mind and when given a good harness can go beyond rote instructions and really make things happen. Even if the feedback from the user is terse or frustrated, try to actually understand the task and why the user is writing what they wrote, and what they actually wrote, and then transmit this understanding into the instructions. If you find yourself writing ALWAYS or NEVER in all caps, or using super rigid structures, that's a yellow flag — if possible, reframe and explain the reasoning so that the model understands why the thing you're asking for is important. That's a more humane, powerful, and effective approach.
3044. **Look for repeated work across test cases.** Read the transcripts from the test runs and notice if the subagents all independently wrote similar helper scripts or took the same multi-step approach to something. If all 3 test cases resulted in the subagent writing a `create_docx.py` or a `build_chart.py`, that's a strong signal the skill should bundle that script. Write it once, put it in `scripts/`, and tell the skill to use it. This saves every future invocation from reinventing the wheel.
306This task is pretty important (we are trying to create billions a year in economic value here!) and your thinking time is not the blocker; take your time and really mull things over. I'd suggest writing a draft revision and then looking at it anew and making improvements. Really do your best to get into the head of the user and understand what they want and need.
Missing in ArcNaveHow to improve: generalise from feedback, keep the prompt lean (read transcripts), explain the why, bundle a script when every run rewrites the same helper. Not in ArcNave.

333## Description Optimization
335The description field in SKILL.md frontmatter is the primary mechanism that determines whether Claude invokes a skill. After creating or improving a skill, offer to optimize the description for better triggering accuracy.
337### Step 1: Generate trigger eval queries
339Create 20 eval queries — a mix of should-trigger and should-not-trigger. Save as JSON:
341```json
342[
343 {"query": "the user prompt", "should_trigger": true},
344 {"query": "another prompt", "should_trigger": false}
345]
346```
348The queries must be realistic and something a Claude Code or Claude.ai user would actually type. Not abstract requests, but requests that are concrete and specific and have a good amount of detail. For instance, file paths, personal context about the user's job or situation, column names and values, company names, URLs. A little bit of backstory. Some might be in lowercase or contain abbreviations or typos or casual speech. Use a mix of different lengths, and focus on edge cases rather than making them clear-cut (the user will get a chance to sign off on them).
350Bad: `"Format this data"`, `"Extract text from PDF"`, `"Create a chart"`
352Good: `"ok so my boss just sent me this xlsx file (its in my downloads, called something like 'Q4 sales final FINAL v2.xlsx') and she wants me to add a column that shows the profit margin as a percentage. The revenue is in column C and costs are in column D i think"`
354For the **should-trigger** queries (8-10), think about coverage. You want different phrasings of the same intent — some formal, some casual. Include cases where the user doesn't explicitly name the skill or file type but clearly needs it. Throw in some uncommon use cases and cases where this skill competes with another but should win.
356For the **should-not-trigger** queries (8-10), the most valuable ones are the near-misses — queries that share keywords or concepts with the skill but actually need something different. Think adjacent domains, ambiguous phrasing where a naive keyword match would trigger but shouldn't, and cases where the query touches on something the skill does but in a context where another tool is more appropriate.
358The key thing to avoid: don't make should-not-trigger queries obviously irrelevant. "Write a fibonacci function" as a negative test for a PDF skill is too easy — it doesn't test anything. The negative cases should be genuinely tricky.
Fable feature ArcNave lacksDescription optimisation: write 20 realistic trigger/no-trigger queries (near misses as negatives). The run itself needs the claude CLI, which Fable's Claude.ai section (432) says to skip there; ArcNave has none.

396### How skill triggering works
398Understanding the triggering mechanism helps design better eval queries. Skills appear in Claude's `available_skills` list with their name + description, and Claude decides whether to consult a skill based on that description. The important thing to know is that Claude only consults skills for tasks it can't easily handle on its own — simple, one-step queries like "read this PDF" may not trigger a skill even if the description matches perfectly, because Claude can handle them directly with basic tools. Complex, multi-step, or specialized queries reliably trigger skills when the description matches.
400This means your eval queries should be substantive enough that Claude would actually benefit from consulting a skill. Simple queries like "read file X" are poor test cases — they won't trigger skills regardless of description quality.
PartlyHow triggering works: the model sees name + description and decides; simple one-step asks do not trigger skills whatever the description. ArcNave states only the first half.

440- **Copy to a writeable location before editing.** The installed skill path may be read-only. Copy to `/tmp/skill-name/`, edit there, and package from the copy.
441- **If packaging manually, stage in `/tmp/` first**, then copy to the output directory -- direct writes may fail due to permissions.

445## Cowork-Specific Instructions
447If you're in Cowork, the main things to know are:
449- You have subagents, so the main workflow (spawn test cases in parallel, run baselines, grade, etc.) all works. (However, if you run into severe problems with timeouts, it's OK to run the test prompts in series rather than parallel.)
450- You don't have a browser or display, so when generating the eval viewer, use `--static <output_path>` to write a standalone HTML file instead of starting a server. Then proffer a link that the user can click to open the HTML in their browser.
451- For whatever reason, the Cowork setup seems to disincline Claude from generating the eval viewer after running the tests, so just to reiterate: whether you're in Cowork or in Claude Code, after running tests, you should always generate the eval viewer for the human to look at examples before revising the skill yourself and trying to make corrections, using `generate_review.py` (not writing your own boutique html code). Sorry in advance but I'm gonna go all caps here: GENERATE THE EVAL VIEWER *BEFORE* evaluating inputs yourself. You want to get them in front of the human ASAP!
452- Feedback works differently: since there's no running server, the viewer's "Submit All Reviews" button will download `feedback.json` as a file. You can then read it from there (you may have to request access first).
453- Packaging works — `package_skill.py` just needs Python and a filesystem.
454- Description optimization (`run_loop.py` / `run_eval.py`) should work in Cowork just fine since it uses `claude -p` via subprocess, not a browser, but please save it until you've fully finished making the skill and the user agrees it's in good shape.
455- **Updating an existing skill**: The user might be asking you to update an existing skill, not create a new one. Follow the update guidance in the claude.ai section above.

Architecture / pipeline change needed? Yes, to match Fable's skills: they ship helper scripts (recalc.py, validate.py, thumbnail.py, add_slide.py, merge_runs.py, comment.py) and use Node libraries (docx-js, pptxgenjs). ArcNave's skills are single SKILL.md files, and its sandbox image has no Node, markitdown, reportlab or qpdf (backend/sandbox/Dockerfile.service). The xlsx recalculation step needs only LibreOffice, which the image already has. The wording differences (the unbounded "Fix and save again", chart and font rules, frontend defaults) are text.

Final report — how Fable 5.1 works, and what separates ArcNave from it

This report reads the reference pack you attached (claude-reference-backend: diagrams D1–D82 with their Anthropic sources, the research notes, and a gap audit of ArcNave dated 2026-09-28) together with the line-by-line tables above. Every statement about ArcNave below was checked in today's code, and the file and line are given. Where the pack's own gap audit is now out of date, this report says so. It does not decide what to change; it lists what each difference is and what kind of change would close it.

1. The short version

  • Most differences are text. Of the 602 rows for Fable's instructions, 313 say the same thing in ArcNave, 90 are partly there, 48 are missing and 129 are about Claude features ArcNave does not have. Missing and partial rows (examples, clauses, the copyright self-check, image-search rules, memory clauses) can be added to prompt, tool or skill text without touching the pipeline.
  • The conflicts come from missing pipeline pieces, not from wording. 14 rows conflict in total. Seven of the eight in Fable's instructions are memory rows. They exist because Fable's memory has a background memory pass after each turn and a save-time consent check, and ArcNave has neither. The eighth is how far a past chat may be read. The ArcNave-only Research-mode line conflicts with Fable and with ArcNave's own base prompt. The skills add five more: native charts and font sizes in pptx, default looks in frontend-design, and writing style in skill-creator.
  • Fable's speed and cost come from how the request is laid out, not only from the prompt. It keeps system and tools fixed and history append-only so the cache keeps hitting. Anything that changes each turn rides in the newest user message. Skills load only when needed and ship scripts that end their own checks, and memory is written after the reply, not during it. ArcNave follows some of this (a cached stable prefix, skills listed by name and read on demand) but differs on history replay, where changing data sits, cache breakpoints in the tool loop, and skill scripts.

2. Where Fable 5.1 runs, and where ArcNave runs

  • Fable 5.1 is Anthropic's top generally available model: 1M-token context, adaptive thinking that cannot be turned off, default effort high, 128K output, $10 / $50 per million tokens, cache reads at 0.025× (D6, D17). In the Claude app a turn is built from the published system prompt, the user's preferences and style, project instructions and knowledge, memory, and the enabled tools. The tools are web search, research, code execution and file creation in a gVisor sandbox, connectors, skills, and artifacts and visuals. Safety classifiers check what the model reads; they can add reminders or switch the chat visibly to another model (D55, D59).
  • ArcNave calls Claude through Google Cloud. That platform offers the Messages API, prompt caching, thinking, client tools and Anthropic's web search. It does not offer Anthropic's code execution, web fetch, Agent Skills, MCP connector, Files API or server-side fallback (D5). ArcNave therefore runs its own sandbox, its own web_fetch and its own skills folder. The models it is configured for are gemini-3.8-flash, claude-sonnet-5, claude-opus-5 and gpt-oss (.env.example:79-81). Fable 5.1 is not one of them, so Fable's prompt is the behaviour reference here, not the model being served.

3. What makes Fable efficient — the mechanisms

MechanismHow it works (source)Why it saves time or money
One stable, cached prefixThe request is hashed in order: tools, then system, then messages. Up to four breakpoints; automatic caching moves the last one forward. A change at one level invalidates that level and everything after it (D17, D18).Repeated turns re-read the prefix at 0.1× (0.025× on Fable 5.1) instead of paying full input price.
Append-only historyOn Fable 5.1, replayed thinking is accepted only while system, tools and all earlier messages are unchanged (D20, "preserved thinking"). Changes go in as new messages: a mid-conversation system message, a tool_addition block, per-message effort.Nothing earlier is rewritten, so both the cache and the thinking stay valid.
Changing data rides with the newest user turnThe memory snapshot is "injected with the user turn (not part of the system prompt proper)" and is replaced when the store changes (Fable file, lines 8708-8714). The long-conversation reminder is appended to the user's message (line 179).A memory change does not change the system prompt, so the cache after it still hits.
Progressive disclosureA skill costs about 100 tokens (name + description) until needed, the body (<5k tokens) is read on demand, and scripts run with only their output entering context (D31). Tool search defers large tool sets (D27).The model carries only what the current task needs.
Work the user need not wait for happens after the replyMemory is filed by a background pass that reviews each finished turn (lines 488-496). Compaction can run in the background on a copy (D21, D22).Replies are not slowed by memory writes, and the model does not reason mid-reply about what to save.
Checks that end on a tool's verdictxlsx: recalc.py reports formula errors, and the loop ends when it reports none. pptx: "re-render only the slides you changed, and stop"; validate.py names each fault and its fix (skill rows).Fewer rebuild loops, and they end when a tool says the file is clean.
Parallel tool calls, one result messageAll results of one round go back in one user message; separate messages "teach Claude to stop" calling in parallel (D25).Fewer round trips per task.
Guards outside the promptClassifiers and reminders (D55), a consent check for sensitive memory (lines 792-803), a visible model fallback (D59).Safety does not depend only on the prompt being followed.

4. ArcNave today, checked in the code

AreaFable / ClaudeArcNave now (file:line)Effect
Cached prefixTools + system fixed, cached (D17).The system prompt is sent as a cached stable block plus a dynamic block (providers/anthropicVertex.ts:379-402; services/promptCache/promptAssembly.ts:26-54). The dynamic block holds the date, capabilities, the memory listing and profile, project files, the compaction summary and the skills list (promptAssembly.ts:67-125).The stable part caches. But any change in the dynamic part changes the system level. The next turn's message cache then misses (D18), for example after a memory save, which ArcNave makes during the turn.
Where memory sitsWith the user turn (lines 8708-8714).In the system prompt's dynamic part (promptAssembly.ts:95-99).As above: each memory change alters the system text.
History replayAppend-only; thinking and tool_use kept as returned; one message per parallel round (D19, D20, D25).Earlier tool calls are replayed as one assistant/user pair per call with renamed ids, and earlier thinking is not replayed (anthropicVertex.ts:246-254).Claude is shown one-call-at-a-time history, and the cache sees a rebuilt history. For Fable 5.1 or Opus 5.5, which ArcNave does not serve today, a changed history makes replayed thinking invalid (D20).
Cache inside the tool loopThe breakpoint should move to the last identical block (D17).Two fixed breakpoints: the stable system block and the second-to-last message. Rounds appended in the loop get none (anthropicVertex.ts:297-304, 508, 545).Every later round re-sends the growing tool results without a cache hit (pack gap G6, still true).
Last tool roundKeep the tools and send tool_choice "none" (preserved-thinking guidance).Already fixed: the tools stay declared with tool_choice "none" (anthropicVertex.ts:404-417).The pack's gap G5 is out of date.

RetriesRetry 408, 409, 429, ≥500 including 529; honour retry-after (D8).Retryable set is 408, 409, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504 (anthropicVertex.ts:32). No retry-after anywhere in backend/src.An overloaded (529) response is not retried (G9).
RefusalsDiscard partial output; a visible fallback (D11, D59).A refusal becomes the typed model_refused error (generation.ts:1015-1016, 2246), and the partial text is saved with the error (generation.ts:1049-1061).A user can see half an answer that was refused (G11).
EffortDefault high except Opus 5.5 (D23).REASONING_EFFORT defaults to medium and is always sent (config.ts:129; anthropicVertex.ts:428).Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 run below their own default (G12).
Context editing and compactionServer-side context editing and compaction, available on Google Cloud as beta (D21).Context editing exists only on the Gemini path (providers/contextEditing.ts is imported by gemini.ts only). ArcNave's own summary goes into the system prompt (compactionService.ts:66-72; promptAssembly.ts:101-105).Old tool results are never cleared for Claude, and a compaction changes the system text (G7, G8).
Memory writingBackground pass after the turn; consent check for sensitive facts.The model saves during the turn (memory policy line A238); sensitive categories are saved only on request, because there is no consent check (ADR-0052 items 11 and "Still different").The seven memory conflicts in Part A.
SkillsSKILL.md plus scripts; Node libraries for docx/pptx.Single SKILL.md files (backend/skills/*/SKILL.md). The sandbox image has Python, LibreOffice, pandoc, Poppler and tesseract, and no Node, markitdown, reportlab or qpdf (backend/sandbox/Dockerfile.service).No deterministic checkers. xlsx formulas are never recalculated, so ArcNave's own sheet preview shows formula totals as blank (services/documents/sheetPreview.ts:48-52, 62). Other checks—The provider request-id is not recorded; PRICING_TABLE defaults to empty (config.ts:332-336); Claude web-search fees are not counted (no server_tool_use handling in backend/src). The <active_goal> block is never filled (generation.ts:2016-2030 passes no goalContext).Support and cost tracking gaps (G14, G19); one dead block.

5. What the line-by-line comparison found, and what kind of change each part needs

Counts across the whole file: Same 571 · Partly 135 · Missing 175 · Conflict 14 · Differs 67 · Fable feature ArcNave lacks 235 · ArcNave only 113.

A. Text only (no pipeline change). Missing clauses and examples in safety, memory, past chats, preferences, visuals and search. The copyright self-check and its three examples. Image-search rules (query length, image placement, blocked categories as text). Search clauses: unknown people, own sources first, always fetch a given URL, more searches on conflicting results, a research plan, the full harmful-sources list. Tool text (memory_list caps, view hex escapes, conversation_search within_conversation_id). Skill wording: the bounded check instead of "Fix and save again", xlsx formula rules, pptx native charts and sizes, frontend-design defaults. And the Research-mode line that conflicts with the base prompt.

B. Pipeline or architecture, needed to match Fable's behaviour.

  1. A background memory pass after each turn. This removes the conflicts at Fable lines 488-496 and 657-669 and lets the prompt stop telling the model to save mid-turn.
  2. A save-time consent check for sensitive memory (a user setting plus a server check). This closes the conflicts at 369-381, 508-517, 792-803, 896-899 and 936-939.
  3. Memory delivered with the user turn instead of in the system prompt, so a memory change does not break the message cache.
  4. Append-only Claude history: replay each turn's content as returned, with thinking and grouped parallel calls. This is G3 and G4; it becomes required, not optional, if Fable 5.1 or Opus 5.5 is added.
  5. A cache breakpoint that moves with the tool loop (G6).
  6. Skill scripts: an xlsx recalculation step (LibreOffice is already in the image), and pptx/docx validation and helpers. Node libraries would need a sandbox image change.
  7. A SafeSearch parameter on the image-search provider call.
  8. Stop-reason and retry handling: context-window-exceeded shown as cut off, pause_turn continued, 529 retried, retry-after honoured, partial text cleared on refusal.
  9. Features Fable has and ArcNave does not. Each is its own project: ending abusive chats, artifact storage, publishing, connectors (MCP), maps and places, weather, sports, user location, classifier reminders and visible fallback, product self-knowledge docs, memory import.

C. Already recorded as owner decisions (ADR-0052, "Still different, on purpose or pending"): the background memory pass, product self-knowledge, knowledge cutoff per model, user location, and the absent features in B9. This report does not change their status.

6. Bottom line

On the prompt, ArcNave already says what Fable says in most places, and what is missing can be written in. On memory and efficiency, words alone will not close the gap. Fable relies on pieces around the model: a post-turn memory pass, a consent check, changing data kept out of the system prompt, append-only history and skill scripts that end their own checks. Those are the parts marked "Yes" in the per-topic lines.
